problem.user_text: An automotive supplier builds 800-volt silicon-carbide traction-inverter power modules whose junction temperature cycles between 45 and 175 degrees Celsius during normal city driving, roughly 300,000 deep cycles over the vehicle life. The die-attach layer between the silicon-carbide die and the direct-bonded-copper substrate progressively delaminates from the die edges inward: measured thermal resistance from junction to baseplate climbs 25 to 40 percent by end of life, junction temperature rise follows, and modules begin exceeding the 175-degree junction limit during 60-second acceleration events well before the vehicle's 15-year design life. Failures cluster when the module sees sustained cornering-grade vibration combined with high-load regeneration, and returned modules show crack patterns initiating at the die corner with the largest solder void. The supplier needs junction-to-baseplate thermal resistance to stay within 10 percent of new-build value across the full 300,000-cycle life, with no increase in module footprint or height (the inverter's power density is fixed), no process step beyond standard power-module assembly lines, die size unchanged, and cost per module held within 8 percent of the current bill of materials.

evidence.title: Advanced Non-Local Pipeline for Domain-Adapted Intelligent Power Device Defects Analysis for a Robust Traction Inverter in Next Generation Electric Cars
evidence.abstract: Silicon Carbide ($S$ iC) power devices are highly sought in modern power electronics for their superior performance; however, yield is severely impacted by crystal-growth defects often termed killer defects. Fast and accurate post-growth inspection of SiC wafers is therefore critical to identify such defects and improve manufacturing outcomes. We propose an improved YOLO-based one-stage detector that integrates a Non-Local Block + Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) module into the YOLO backbone between the Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP) and BottleneckCSP layers. The Non-Local blocks enable the CNN to leverage global context in the microscopic images, improving its ability to recognize subtle defect patterns across the wafer. Meanwhile, the GRL-based domain adaptation allows the model to learn domain-invariant features, addressing distribution shifts between different datasets or imaging conditions. The proposed architecture, comprising these components, is evaluated on a dataset of SiC wafer optical micrographs containing various defect types to demonstrate its effectiveness (e.g., dislocations and stacking faults). The proposed method achieves mAP@0.5=95% and mAP@0.5:0.95=94.5%. These improvements demonstrate the efficacy of combining attention and adversarial domain adaptation in the YOLO architecture. The enhanced model detects $S$ iC defects with higher accuracy and robustness to varying imaging conditions, marking a significant step forward in automated wafer defect inspection.

evidence.title: Silicon Carbide Multi-Chip Power Module for Traction Inverter Applications: Thermal Characterization and Modeling
evidence.abstract: Semiconductor power modules are the key hardware components of a traction inverter. It drives motor speed and torque, managing the energy exchange from battery to motor and viceversa. The increasing demand for electric and hybrid vehicle requests high performance power modules. Power semiconductor devices based on wide band gap compound, like silicon carbide (SiC), have excellent electrical properties in terms of on-state resistance, stray inductance and performance at high commutation frequency. One of the most promising solution is silicon carbide MOSFET power module in which each switch is made by several different dies placed in parallel. Embedded direct cooling system and novel materials with high conductivity (e.g., active metal brazed substrates) can be considered to enhance thermal performance. A robust method is needed to characterize and to predict power module temperature behavior considering the importance of the thermal performance to improve reliability and to optimize module weight and dimensions. According to several parallel dies inside each switch, classic method based on temperature electric sensitive parameter (TSEP) shall be validated with direct measurement. In this framework, it has been reported the thermal characterization of a power module for a traction inverter based on eight silicon carbide MOSFETs for each switch. Both TSEP and infrared measurements have been employed. Thermal behavior has been numerically reproduced, creating a simplified equivalent network and developing a predictive model by finite element method (FEM)

evidence.title: Design and Analysis of PCB Embedded SiC Half-Bridge Packaging Cells With Low Thermal Resistance and Parasitic Inductance
evidence.abstract: Reducing parasitic parameters and thermal resistance is critical for advancing power electronic devices. This article designs and evaluates the three printed circuit board (PCB) embedded 1200 V SiC mosfet half-bridge packaging cells, where the traditional wire bonding process is replaced by a redistribution layer (RDL) technique. A comprehensive evaluation of their electrical performance, thermal management, and mechanical performance is conducted. The three solutions that employ panel, active metal brazing (AMB), and lead—frame carriers, are developed through a streamlined process that includes die attach, molding, drilling, plating, and etching. This packaging approach readily reduces the parasitic inductance to below 5 nH. By utilizing a single-layer RDL with mutual inductance cancellation, the power loop inductance is reduced to as low as 2.4 nH (at 10 MHz), and the gate loop inductance to 1.57 nH (at 10 MHz). The junction-to-case thermal resistances of the three solutions are 1.88, 1.03, and 0.73 K/W, respectively. Compared with the other two packaging cells, the cell selecting AMB as a carrier reduces SiC mosfet operational stress and deformation by approximately 34% and 75% . The lead—frame carrier offers superior thermal dissipation for potential TO package replacement in half-bridge topologies, while the panel solution is promising for dual-sided cooling applications. With low thermal resistance, minimal stress, and excellent backside electrical insulation, the packaging cell with an AMB carrier is ideally suited for integration with heatsinks in traction inverters.

evidence.title: Thermal Coupling Characterization of a Multi-Chip SiC Power Module
evidence.abstract: In multichip silicon carbide (SiC) power modules, thermal interaction among paralleled dies significantly constrains usable current capability. This paper presents an electro-thermal FEA framework to characterize self-heating and die-to-die mutual heating in a multi-chip SiC half-bridge module. A full thermal impedance matrix is extracted via sequential unit-power excitation, incorporating layout-consistent indexing to systematically resolve intra-leg, cross-leg, and DBC-partition effects. To address metric ambiguity, heating matrices based on peak temperature and average junction temperatures are established and compared. Eigenmode decomposition reveals that the dominant common-mode impedance is 2.5 times higher than the single-die self-heating impedance, with mutual heating contributing approximately 60% to the total temperature rise, including a non-negligible 12% -13% originating from cross-leg coupling. Furthermore, quantitative analysis demonstrates that thermal models calibrated on die-averaged temperatures systematically underestimate self-heating impedance by 9.2% and worst-case system impedance by 7.7%. These findings confirm that while average-temperature metrics suffice for relative layout optimization, a hotspot-based full matrix approach is indispensable for accurate safety margin determination and reliability prediction.

evidence.title: Electrified Powertrain SiC Inverter Loss Sensitivity to Design and Operation Parameter Assumptions
evidence.abstract: Silicon-Carbide (SiC) power semiconductors have not yet deeply penetrated into electrified powertrain applications due to the challenges in achieving cost competitiveness and in answering reliability questions. It has, however, already been shown by numerous studies that SiC devices can offer advantages, for example, significantly lower inverter power losses than Si devices. This paper attempts, then, not to make SiC vs. Si comparison, but to estimate how sensitive electrified powertrain SiC inverter losses are to the design and operation parameter assumptions. Various parameters, including device voltage rating, switching frequency, total active die-size, junction temperature, with-and-without external Schottky barrier diodes, are considered. The SiC inverter loss landscapes were generated and observations were made with those landscapes, including loss maps over the motor torque-speed plane.

evidence.title: Energy Optimal Switching Frequency for a 750V Metro Traction Drive Using Silicon Carbide MOSFET Inverter
evidence.abstract: The introduction of Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFET based inverters into the traction drive makes it possible to increase the inverter switching frequency and reduce energy consumption. This paper describes how to model switching frequency dependent losses in the traction drive and compares the calculated losses to measurements done on a newly developed SiC MOSFET based traction drive. The results from the developed loss models of motor and inverter agrees well with the results from energy measurements. This paper concludes that the energy use of the traction motor and inverter can be simulated well using simple models where skin-effect losses in the motor are modelled in detailed. This paper also concludes that in terms of energy efficiency, the optimal switching frequency using a SiC MOSFET based inverter, is in the range of 3-6 kHz. </p

evidence.title: A quantitative assessment of nanometric machinability of major polytypes of single crystal silicon carbide
evidence.abstract: The influence of polymorphism on nanometric machinability of single crystal silicon carbide (SiC) has been investigated through molecular dynamics (MD) simulation. The simulation results are compared with silicon as a reference material. Cutting hardness was adopted as a quantifier of the machinability of the polytypes of single crystal SiC. 3C-SiC offered highest cutting resistance (∼2.9 times that of silicon) followed by the 4H-SiC (∼2.8 times that of silicon) whereas 6H-SiC (∼2.1 times that of silicon) showed the least. Despite its high cutting resistance, 4H-SiC showed the minimum sub-surface crystal lattice deformed layer depth, in contrast to 6H-SiC. Further analysis of temperatures in the cutting zone and the percentage tool wear indicated that single point diamond turning (SPDT) of single crystal SiC could be limited to either 6H-SiC or 4H-SiC depending upon quality and cost considerations as these were found to be more responsive and amenable to SPDT compared to single crystal 3C-SiC

items.record_text: Thermal Coupling Characterization of a Multi-Chip SiC Power Module In multichip silicon carbide (SiC) power modules, thermal interaction among paralleled dies significantly constrains usable current capability. This paper presents an electro-thermal FEA framework to characterize self-heating and die-to-die mutual heating in a multi-chip SiC half-bridge module. A full thermal impedance matrix is extracted via sequential unit-power excitation, incorporating layout-consistent indexing to systematically resolve intra-leg, cross-leg, and DBC-partition effects. To address metric ambiguity, heating matrices based on peak temperature and average junction temperatures are established and compared. Eigenmode decomposition reveals that the dominant common-mode impedance is 2.5 times higher than the single-die self-heating impedance, with mutual heating contributing approximately 60% to the total temperature rise, including a non-negligible 12% -13% originating from cross-leg coupling. Furthermore, quantitative analysis demonstrates that thermal models calibrated on die-averaged temperatures systematically underestimate self-heating impedance by 9.2% and worst-case system impedance by 7.7%. These findings confirm that while average-temperature metrics suffice for relative layout optimization, a hotspot-based full matrix approach is indispensable for accurate safety margin determination and reliability prediction.

It has, however, already been shown by numerous studies that SiC devices can offer advantages, for example, significantly lower inverter power losses than Si devices. This paper attempts, then, not to make SiC vs. Si comparison, but to estimate how sensitive electrified powertrain SiC inverter losses are to the design and operation parameter assumptions. items.record_text: A quantitative assessment of nanometric machinability of major polytypes of single crystal silicon carbide The influence of polymorphism on nanometric machinability of single crystal silicon carbide (SiC) has been investigated through molecular dynamics (MD) simulation. The simulation results are compared with silicon as a reference material. Cutting hardness was adopted as a quantifier of the machinability of the polytypes of single crystal SiC. 3C-SiC offered highest cutting resistance (∼2.9 times that of silicon) followed by the 4H-SiC (∼2.8 times that of silicon) whereas 6H-SiC (∼2.1 times that of silicon) showed the least. Despite its high cutting resistance, 4H-SiC showed the minimum sub-surface crystal lattice deformed layer depth, in contrast to 6H-SiC. Further analysis of temperatures in the cutting zone and the percentage tool wear indicated that single point diamond turning (SPDT) of single crystal SiC could be limited to either 6H-SiC or 4H-SiC depending upon quality and cost considerations as these were found to be more responsive and amenable to SPDT compared to single crystal 3C-SiC

items.record_text: Advanced Non-Local Pipeline for Domain-Adapted Intelligent Power Device Defects Analysis for a Robust Traction Inverter in Next Generation Electric Cars Silicon Carbide ($S$ iC) power devices are highly sought in modern power electronics for their superior performance; however, yield is severely impacted by crystal-growth defects often termed killer defects. Fast and accurate post-growth inspection of SiC wafers is therefore critical to identify such defects and improve manufacturing outcomes. We propose an improved YOLO-based one-stage detector that integrates a Non-Local Block + Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) module into the YOLO backbone between the Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP) and BottleneckCSP layers. The Non-Local blocks enable the CNN to leverage global context in the microscopic images, improving its ability to recognize subtle defect patterns across the wafer. Meanwhile, the GRL-based domain adaptation allows the model to learn domain-invariant features, addressing distribution shifts between different datasets or imaging conditions. The proposed architecture, comprising these components, is evaluated on a dataset of SiC wafer optical micrographs containing various defect types to demonstrate its effectiveness (e.g., dislocations and stacking faults). The proposed method achieves mAP@0.5=95% and mAP@0.5:0.95=94.5%. These improvements demonstrate the efficacy of combining attention and adversarial domain adaptation in the YOLO architecture. The enhanced model detects $S$ iC defects with higher accuracy and robustness to varying imaging conditions, marking a significant step forward in automated wafer defect inspection.

items.record_text: Design and Analysis of PCB Embedded SiC Half-Bridge Packaging Cells With Low Thermal Resistance and Parasitic Inductance Reducing parasitic parameters and thermal resistance is critical for advancing power electronic devices. This article designs and evaluates the three printed circuit board (PCB) embedded 1200 V SiC mosfet half-bridge packaging cells, where the traditional wire bonding process is replaced by a redistribution layer (RDL) technique. A comprehensive evaluation of their electrical performance, thermal management, and mechanical performance is conducted. The three solutions that employ panel, active metal brazing (AMB), and lead—frame carriers, are developed through a streamlined process that includes die attach, molding, drilling, plating, and etching. This packaging approach readily reduces the parasitic inductance to below 5 nH. By utilizing a single-layer RDL with mutual inductance cancellation, the power loop inductance is reduced to as low as 2.4 nH (at 10 MHz), and the gate loop inductance to 1.57 nH (at 10 MHz). The junction-to-case thermal resistances of the three solutions are 1.88, 1.03, and 0.73 K/W, respectively. Compared with the other two packaging cells, the cell selecting AMB as a carrier reduces SiC mosfet operational stress and deformation by approximately 34% and 75% . The lead—frame carrier offers superior thermal dissipation for potential TO package replacement in half-bridge topologies, while the panel solution is promising for dual-sided cooling applications. With low thermal resistance, minimal stress, and excellent backside electrical insulation, the packaging cell with an AMB carrier is ideally suited for integration with heatsinks in traction inverters.

custody_records.raw_content: Silicon Carbide ($S$ iC) power devices are highly sought in modern power electronics for their superior performance; however, yield is severely impacted by crystal-growth defects often termed killer defects. Fast and accurate post-growth inspection of SiC wafers is therefore critical to identify such defects and improve manufacturing outcomes. We propose an improved YOLO-based one-stage detector that integrates a Non-Local Block + Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) module into the YOLO backbone between the Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP) and BottleneckCSP layers. The Non-Local blocks enable the CNN to leverage global context in the microscopic images, improving its ability to recognize subtle defect patterns across the wafer. Meanwhile, the GRL-based domain adaptation allows the model to learn domain-invariant features, addressing distribution shifts between different datasets or imaging conditions. The proposed architecture, comprising these components, is evaluated on a dataset of SiC wafer optical micrographs containing various defect types to demonstrate its effectiveness (e.g., dislocations and stacking faults). The proposed method achieves mAP@0.5=95% and mAP@0.5:0.95=94.5%. These improvements demonstrate the efficacy of combining attention and adversarial domain adaptation in the YOLO architecture. The enhanced model detects $S$ iC defects with higher accuracy and robustness to varying imaging conditions, marking a significant step forward in automated wafer defect inspection.

It drives motor speed and torque, managing the energy exchange from battery to motor and viceversa. The increasing demand for electric and hybrid vehicle requests high performance power modules. Power semiconductor devices based on wide band gap compound, like silicon carbide (SiC), have excellent electrical properties in terms of on-state resistance, stray inductance and performance at high commutation frequency. One of the most promising solution is silicon carbide MOSFET power module in which each switch is made by several different dies placed in parallel. Embedded direct cooling system and novel materials with high conductivity (e.g., active metal brazed substrates) can be considered to enhance thermal performance. A robust method is needed to characterize and to predict power module temperature behavior considering the importance of the thermal performance to improve reliability and to optimize module weight and dimensions. According to several parallel dies inside each switch, classic method based on temperature electric sensitive parameter (TSEP) shall be validated with direct measurement. In this framework, it has been reported the thermal characterization of a power module for a traction inverter based on eight silicon carbide MOSFETs for each switch. Both TSEP and infrared measurements have been employed. Thermal behavior has been numerically reproduced, creating a simplified equivalent network and developing a predictive model by finite element method (FEM)

custody_records.raw_content: Reducing parasitic parameters and thermal resistance is critical for advancing power electronic devices. This article designs and evaluates the three printed circuit board (PCB) embedded 1200 V SiC mosfet half-bridge packaging cells, where the traditional wire bonding process is replaced by a redistribution layer (RDL) technique. A comprehensive evaluation of their electrical performance, thermal management, and mechanical performance is conducted. The three solutions that employ panel, active metal brazing (AMB), and lead—frame carriers, are developed through a streamlined process that includes die attach, molding, drilling, plating, and etching. This packaging approach readily reduces the parasitic inductance to below 5 nH. By utilizing a single-layer RDL with mutual inductance cancellation, the power loop inductance is reduced to as low as 2.4 nH (at 10 MHz), and the gate loop inductance to 1.57 nH (at 10 MHz). The junction-to-case thermal resistances of the three solutions are 1.88, 1.03, and 0.73 K/W, respectively. Compared with the other two packaging cells, the cell selecting AMB as a carrier reduces SiC mosfet operational stress and deformation by approximately 34% and 75% . The lead—frame carrier offers superior thermal dissipation for potential TO package replacement in half-bridge topologies, while the panel solution is promising for dual-sided cooling applications. With low thermal resistance, minimal stress, and excellent backside electrical insulation, the packaging cell with an AMB carrier is ideally suited for integration with heatsinks in traction inverters.

custody_records.raw_content: In multichip silicon carbide (SiC) power modules, thermal interaction among paralleled dies significantly constrains usable current capability. This paper presents an electro-thermal FEA framework to characterize self-heating and die-to-die mutual heating in a multi-chip SiC half-bridge module. A full thermal impedance matrix is extracted via sequential unit-power excitation, incorporating layout-consistent indexing to systematically resolve intra-leg, cross-leg, and DBC-partition effects. To address metric ambiguity, heating matrices based on peak temperature and average junction temperatures are established and compared. Eigenmode decomposition reveals that the dominant common-mode impedance is 2.5 times higher than the single-die self-heating impedance, with mutual heating contributing approximately 60% to the total temperature rise, including a non-negligible 12% -13% originating from cross-leg coupling. Furthermore, quantitative analysis demonstrates that thermal models calibrated on die-averaged temperatures systematically underestimate self-heating impedance by 9.2% and worst-case system impedance by 7.7%. These findings confirm that while average-temperature metrics suffice for relative layout optimization, a hotspot-based full matrix approach is indispensable for accurate safety margin determination and reliability prediction.

It has, however, already been shown by numerous studies that SiC devices can offer advantages, for example, significantly lower inverter power losses than Si devices. This paper attempts, then, not to make SiC vs. Si comparison, but to estimate how sensitive electrified powertrain SiC inverter losses are to the design and operation parameter assumptions. Various parameters, including device voltage rating, switching frequency, total active die-size, junction temperature, with-and-without external Schottky barrier diodes, are considered. The SiC inverter loss landscapes were generated and observations were made with those landscapes, including loss maps over the motor torque-speed plane.

Cutting hardness was adopted as a quantifier of the machinability of the polytypes of single crystal SiC. 3C-SiC offered highest cutting resistance (∼2.9 times that of silicon) followed by the 4H-SiC (∼2.8 times that of silicon) whereas 6H-SiC (∼2.1 times that of silicon) showed the least.
